title: Armour
description: Covering used to protect from physical injury or damage
wiki_lead:
Armour (Commonwealth English) or armor (American English; see spelling differences) is a covering used to protect an object, individual, or vehicle from physical injury or damage, especially direct contact weapons or projectiles during combat, or from a potentially dangerous environment or activity (e.g. cycling, construction sites, etc.).  Personal armour is used to protect soldiers and war animals. Vehicle armour is used on warships, armoured fighting vehicles, and some combat aircraft, mostly ground attack aircraft.
A second use of the term armour describes armoured forces, armoured weapons, and their role in combat. After the development of armoured warfare, tanks and mechanised infantry and their combat formations came to be referred to collectively as "armour".

Personal armour is used to protect soldiers and war animals. Vehicle armour is used on warships, armoured fighting vehicles, and some combat aircraft, mostly ground attack aircraft.
A second use of the term armour describes armoured forces, armoured weapons, and their role in combat. After the development of armoured warfare, tanks and mechanised infantry and their combat formations came to be referred to collectively as "armour".


Etymology

The word "armour" began to appear in the Middle Ages as a derivative of Old French. It is dated from 1297 as a "mail, defensive covering worn in combat". The word originates from the Old French armure, itself derived from the Latin armatura meaning "arms and/or equipment", with the root armare meaning "arms or gear".


History


Personal

Armour has been used throughout recorded history. It has been made from a variety of materials, beginning with the use of leathers or fabrics as protection and evolving through chain mail and metal plate into today's modern composites. For much of military history the manufacture of metal personal armour has dominated the technology and employment of armour.
Armour drove the development of many important technologies of the Ancient World, including wood lamination, mining, metal refining, vehicle manufacture, leather processing, and later decorative metal working. Its production was influential in the Industrial Revolution, and furthered commercial development of metallurgy and engineering.  Armour was also an important factor in the development of firearms, which in turn revolutionized warfare. Originally, armor was worn by those thought to be the holiest and therefore the highest on social / religious hierarchies. Armor, especially linked armor (soon to become chainmail) was worn by high society as “loricati’ (anatomical chest plates which sculpted the perfect male trunk) which exemplified honor, pride, and an urge to do good for their sins. In ancient times, concerning monks, the concept of a knight or man clad in armor was actually negative because it harbinged symbols of death and violence -- which is not far off from how armor came to be utilized.


History

Significant factors in the development of armour include the economic and technological necessities of its production. For instance, plate armour became widespread in Medieval Europe when water-powered trip hammers made the forming of plates faster and cheaper. At times the development of armour has paralleled the development of increasingly effective weaponry on the battlefield, with armourers seeking to create better protection without sacrificing mobility.
Well-known armour types in European history include the  lorica squamata and the lorica segmentata of the Roman legions, the mail hauberk of the early medieval age, and the full steel plate harness worn by later medieval and renaissance knights, and breast and back plates worn by heavy cavalry in several European countries until the first year of World War I (1914–1915). 
A well known example in Europe of Asian armour are the many types of armour used by warriors of Feudal Japan for hundreds of years up to the 19th century. 


Early

The first record of body armour in history was found on the Stele of Vultures in ancient Sumer in today's south Iraq, and various forms of scale mail can be seen in surviving records from the New Kingdom of Egypt, Zhou dynasty China, and dynastic India. Cuirasses and helmets were manufactured in Japan as early as the 4th century. Tankō, worn by foot soldiers and keikō, worn by horsemen were both pre-samurai types of early Japanese armour constructed from iron plates connected together by leather thongs. Japanese lamellar armour (keiko) passed through Korea and reached Japan around the 5th century. These early Japanese lamellar armours took the form of a sleeveless jacket, leggings and a helmet.
Armour did not always cover all of the body; sometimes no more than a helmet and leg plates were worn. The rest of the body was generally protected by means of a large shield. An example of armies equipping their troops in this fashion were the Aztecs (13th to 15th century CE).
In East Asia, many types of armour were commonly used at different times by various cultures, including scale armour, lamellar armour, laminar armour, plated mail, mail, plate armour, and brigandine.Around the dynastic Tang, Song, and early Ming Period, cuirasses and plates (mingguangjia) were also used, with more elaborate versions for officers in war. The Chinese, during that time used partial plates for "important" body parts instead of covering their whole body since too much plate armour hinders their martial arts movement. The other body parts were covered in cloth, leather, lamellar, or mountain pattern armour. In pre-Qin dynasty times, leather armour was made out of various animals, with more exotic ones such as the rhinoceros
Mail, sometimes called "chainmail", made of interlocking iron rings is believed to have first appeared some time after 300 BC. Its invention is credited to the Celts; the Romans are thought to have adopted their design.
Gradually, small additional plates or discs of iron were added to the mail to protect vulnerable areas. Hardened leather and splinted construction were used for arm and leg pieces. The coat of plates was developed, an armour made of large plates sewn inside a textile or leather coat.

grok_lead: Armour is a form of personal protective equipment worn to safeguard the body against weapons and physical trauma, primarily in warfare but also in tournaments, hunting, and ceremonial contexts, constructed from materials ranging from leather and textiles to iron, steel, and alloys. The word "armour" derives from Old French armeÃ¼re, from Latin armÄtÅ«ra meaning "arms" or "equipments". Its design has evolved to balance mobility, coverage, and defense, with early examples featuring simple shields and helmets, progressing to complex full-body suits by the late Middle Ages. The history of armour begins in ancient times, with one of the earliest known metal body armours dating to around 1500 B.C. in Egypt, where warriors wore shirt-like garments reinforced with overlapping bronze scales or plates for protection against arrows and blades. By the 8th century B.C., Greek hoplites adopted bronze cuirasses, greaves, and large round shields ( aspis) to form phalanx formations, emphasizing collective defense in infantry combat. The Romans, from the 3rd century B.C., incorporated Celtic-invented mail ( lorica hamata)âinterlinked iron rings providing flexible coverageâand later the segmented lorica segmentata in the 1st century A.D., which used hinged iron plates for torso protection, weighing about 20â30 pounds. In medieval Europe, armour transitioned from knee-length mail hauberks (by the 11th century, as depicted in the Bayeux Tapestry of 1066) to hybrid forms in the 12thâ13th centuries, incorporating iron plates over mail for limbs and torsos to counter piercing weapons like crossbows. Full plate armour emerged in the 14th century, becoming widespread by 1420, with suits covering the wearer from head to toe (cap-Ã -pie) and weighing around 45â65 pounds, crafted from tempered steel for knights in mounted shock combat during events like the Hundred Years' War (1337â1453). Key components included the bascinet helmet with visor, breastplate, and gauntlets, often customized by renowned centers in northern Italy and southern Germany, such as Milan under the Missaglia family in the 15th century. Renaissance developments (15thâ16th centuries) refined these with lighter, proofed steel against early firearms, while specialized tournament and parade armours incorporated decorative elements like gilding and etching for status display. The advent of gunpowder weapons, such as the arquebus in the 15th century and muskets by the 16th, gradually rendered heavy plate obsolete for battlefield use, shifting focus to lighter forms like corselets ( breastplate and backplate, about 35 pounds) and helmets (morion or cabasset) for infantry, while full suits persisted in ceremonial roles. Today, modern body armour draws from these traditions but employs advanced materials like Kevlar and ceramics to stop bullets, reflecting ongoing adaptations to contemporary threats in military and law enforcement contexts.
